title: Your video did not lose because it was bad. It lost before anyone knew what it was.
markdown:
# Your video did not lose because it was bad. It lost before anyone knew what it was.

At 9:14, you watch your new Reel once more before posting. The lighting is clean. The advice is useful. You have trimmed the pauses. Still, the first sentence is: "Today I want to share three tips for..."

That sentence asks a stranger to wait for the point. On a feed built around a thumb moving every second, waiting is a hard sell.

The first three seconds do not need to explain your whole video. They need to make the next second feel worth taking. That is a narrower job, and it changes how you write.

## Start with the moment your viewer recognizes

Generic openings describe the creator's plan. A workable hook describes the viewer's situation.

Suppose you teach freelancers how to price small projects. "Three pricing tips for freelancers" is accurate, but it gives no reason to pause. The person watching may not yet think they need pricing tips.

Try a moment instead:

> "If clients say yes instantly, your quote may be too low."

Now the viewer can test the line against a recent memory. That small act of recognition creates the pause. The rest of the video can earn the claim, qualify it, or offer a fix.

Before writing a hook, name one scene your viewer has lived through. A creator might write: "I post tutorials, get views, and nobody saves them." A coach might write: "People ask for the link, then disappear after the price." A local business might write: "The camera is rolling, but the owner keeps explaining the menu."

Those are raw materials. They are more useful than a broad topic because they give you something a viewer can immediately recognize.

## Give one idea several entrances

You do not need five different videos to test five hooks. Take one useful point and approach it from different directions.

For a video about fixing a weak opening, the point might be: lead with a specific viewer problem, not an introduction. Here are five ways into that same point:

- **Callout, spoken:** "Creators, your intro is giving people permission to leave."  
  **On-screen text:** Your intro is the exit sign

- **Curiosity, spoken:** "The sentence that kills a good video is usually the first one."  
  **On-screen text:** Watch the first sentence

- **Result, spoken:** "I replaced my intro with one viewer problem. The script got shorter."  
  **On-screen text:** Start with their problem

- **Contrarian, spoken:** "Stop opening with what your video is about."  
  **On-screen text:** Do not announce the topic

- **Stakes, spoken:** "If your hook needs context, the swipe has already won."  
  **On-screen text:** Context comes later

Each one promises a slightly different payoff. The callout is blunt. Curiosity asks for a reveal. The contrarian version creates tension with common advice. None needs a made-up statistic to work.

The strongest choice depends on the footage and the audience, but the hook must still match the body. If you open with a warning about intros, show an intro and revise it. A hook that changes the subject may win a pause, then lose the viewer you just borrowed.

## Write the screen and the voice as a pair

Many short videos have only one hook because the spoken line and the text on screen repeat each other word for word. Let them share the job instead.

The voice can carry the turn: "Your intro is giving people permission to leave." The text can make the point scannable: "Your intro is the exit sign." A viewer watching without sound still gets the tension. A viewer listening gets the fuller thought.

Keep the spoken line short enough to say at a normal pace. If it takes two breaths, it probably takes too long. Put only the words that matter on screen. The screen is not a transcript.

## Build the rest so the hook keeps its promise

Here is a 30-second structure for the same lesson.

**0:00 to 0:03**  
Spoken: "Stop opening with what your video is about."  
On-screen: Do not announce the topic

**0:03 to 0:09**  
Show the weak version: "Today I want to share three tips for stronger hooks."  
Then say: "That makes the viewer wait for the reason to care."

**0:09 to 0:18**  
Show the rewrite: "If people leave before your first tip, this is probably why."  
On-screen: Name the problem first

**0:18 to 0:26**  
Explain the rule: "Start with a moment they recognize, then show the fix."

**0:26 to 0:30**  
Give the next action: "Rewrite your first line as a problem your viewer has felt."

This is not a magic formula. It is a way to make a testable opening without losing the useful part of your video. Film two versions when you can. Change the opening while keeping the body steady, then learn from the response instead of guessing which change mattered.

## When the blank first line is the real bottleneck

The hard part is often not knowing the rule. It is producing enough specific options for one topic, in the right voice, before the filming window disappears.

The next time a video stalls, do not begin by rewriting every sentence. Put the first three seconds under a microscope. That is enough to make the next version worth filming.
